title: Financial Technology and the Green Transition
subtitle: Digital Capital Mobilization, Sustainable Investment, and Emerging-Market Development
dek: Why rapid digital payment adoption in emerging markets has not yet closed the climate-capital gap—and how coupling digital public infrastructure, PAYGO clean-energy telemetry, tokenized sovereign green bonds, and parametric polycrisis insurance mobilizes long-tenor green capital to 2050.
abstract: Over the past fifteen years, emerging and developing economies (EMDEs) achieved an unprecedented retail financial leapfrog. Drawing on thirteen live empirical datasets spanning twenty-four economies (2000–2025)—including World Bank Global Findex, WDI financial depth, branch density, clean cooking, and electricity series alongside Ember/OWID grid decarbonization records—this monograph documents how mobile money and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) pushed adult account ownership to 90.1% in Kenya, 89.0% in India, 86.4% in Brazil, 81.2% in Ghana, and 72.8% in Uganda despite sparse physical banking networks (2.1–5.9 branches per 100,000 adults). Yet these digital rails expose a profound Green-FinTech Mobilization Gap: retail payment velocity has not translated into deep, long-tenor domestic climate capital. Across Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, private domestic credit remains shallow (7.9%–34.5% of GDP), weighted average costs of capital for clean energy remain prohibitive (11%–15%), and clean-cooking access lags far behind both clean grids and mobile-money penetration (2.0% in Uganda, 7.0% in Ethiopia, 32.0% in Kenya).

Operationalizing H Heuristics' Polycrisis Resilience and Intersectional Engineering framework, this study engineers the institutional stack required to convert retail digital rails into resilient green capital formation. It analyzes five high-leverage mechanisms—DPI green liquidity routing, PAYGO e-Cooking and solar-microgrid carbon telemetry, tokenized sovereign green and sustainability-linked bonds, automated parametric polycrisis climate insurance, and digital MRV for high-integrity carbon markets—while auditing second-order maladaptation traps including predatory digital nano-lending, ESG greenwashing, speculative proof-of-work energy drain, and gender digital exclusion (up to -11.0 percentage points in Nigeria and -9.9 pp in Bangladesh). Blended FinTech de-risking compresses emerging-market clean-asset WACC by up to 740 basis points (13.8% to 6.4%), and 2050 scenario modeling shows synchronized green FinTech lifts emerging-market green capital resilience to 286 (2024=100), versus 164 under fragmented retail rails and 84 under predatory debt and climate lock-in.
findings: Quantifies the Green-FinTech Mobilization Gap across 24 economies (2000–2025), contrasting branchless digital account surges (+47.8 to +53.8 pp) against shallow domestic credit (7.9%–34.5% of GDP) and clean-cooking deficits.

Models a 740 bps WACC compression waterfall (13.8% to 6.4%) uniting concessional first-loss guarantees, local-currency DPI liquidity, IoT/PAYGO credit telemetry, parametric climate triggers, and tokenized green bonds.

Maps 2nd- through 4th-order Cross-System Spillovers across decarbonization, gender financial inclusion parity (-11.0 pp to +6.9 pp), public health, grid peak-load decoupling, informal MSME productivity, and sovereign stability.

Audits four maladaptation traps—predatory digital debt, ESG greenwashing, proof-of-work crypto electricity drain, and basis-risk insurance failure—and delivers a 2026–2050 Cross-Regional Operationalization Matrix.
method: Empirical synthesis using verified World Bank WDI and international datasets, peer-reviewed literature, H Heuristics Cross-System Spillover (2nd–4th order) mapping, maladaptation guardrails, and quantitative 2050 polycrisis scenarios.
